title: Burial archaeology and respectful interpretation
summary: Burial evidence can illuminate health and mortuary practice without reducing people to specimens or spectacle. Harappa's cemetery research requires both analytical precision and ethical care.

body.text: A burial is evidence of a person and of the actions taken around that person after death. Archaeological interpretation needs to hold those two dimensions together. Questions about health, burial position or associated objects do not remove the responsibility to describe human remains with care.
What a study's sample can tell us

Nancy Lovell's research on material excavated at Harappa's Cemetery R37 in 1987 and 1988 distinguishes the minimum number of individuals represented from the much smaller number of complete skeletons in primary contexts. That distinction is important before any reported condition is treated as a statement about the whole population.

The study examines several categories of skeletal change, including joint disease and trauma. A finding belongs to a particular examined sample. It should not be inflated into a complete biography for an individual or a sweeping diagnosis of everyone who lived at Harappa. The surviving material and the questions asked of it define the limits of the account.

Burial arrangements require similar restraint. The presence of objects in a grave can be documented, but their relationship with status, belief or personal identity needs an argument. A richer-looking burial is not automatically evidence of a named social rank. The actions of those arranging a burial also need not reproduce every aspect of the deceased person's life.
Respect changes presentation

The Metropolitan Museum's stewardship policy treats human remains as those of once-living people and recognises responsibilities towards living communities. UCL's policy likewise emphasises practical and ethical preparation for people handling such material. These are institutional approaches, not a substitute for Pakistani law or a universal answer to every local question.

Their relevance to a public archive is nevertheless direct. An article can explain a research result without using a sensational photograph. It can distinguish an observation from an emotionally charged reconstruction. It can also acknowledge that display, research access and cultural expectations may require different decisions in different contexts.

Terminology matters. Describing a burial as “mysterious” may attract attention while obscuring the actual problem: incomplete preservation, uncertain association or an unresolved interpretation. Naming the evidential limitation is usually more useful than making the person an object of intrigue.
Keep the research history visible

A cemetery may be excavated in several campaigns, with material subsequently studied using different methods. An account should identify which campaign and sample a conclusion concerns. Changes in classification or interpretation can then be understood as part of continuing research rather than contradictions to conceal.

At Harappa, burial archaeology contributes to understanding lived experience as well as funerary practice. Its value does not depend on reconstructing intimate stories that the evidence cannot support. Careful language, sample-specific claims and respectful presentation allow readers to encounter the research without forgetting that the material belongs to human lives.

title: Historic archaeology after the ancient period
summary: Archaeology does not stop when written records begin. Medieval settlements and later buildings can reveal histories that documents record differently or leave unmentioned.

body.text: Archaeology is often imagined as the study of periods before writing. Once chronicles, inscriptions or administrative records appear, it may seem that historians can take over and the ground has little more to add. That division misunderstands what material evidence can do.
Documents do not describe everything

The Society for Historical Archaeology defines its field through the study of material remains alongside other historical evidence. Written and physical records can illuminate the same setting, but they do not necessarily preserve the same people, activities or priorities.

A text might describe a foundation, a patron or a political event. Surviving fabric can raise questions about subsequent alteration, everyday use or an arrangement omitted from the written account. Neither source should automatically be treated as a transparent account of the other.

Brahmanabad-Mansurah provides a Pakistani point of entry into this discussion. The Department of Archaeology and Museums records the remains of a fortified city. A fortification is not only an illustration for a historical name: its construction, changes and relationship with the surrounding settlement are material questions that require investigation.

This article does not assign a new chronology to that site. Its purpose is to explain why a known historical setting still needs archaeological analysis rather than being considered fully understood once it has been linked with a text.
Agreement is not the only useful result

Suppose a written description presents a building as a single foundation, while its fabric contains several identifiable phases. That difference might reflect later rebuilding, a text's selective purpose or an error in the assumed association. It should prompt research rather than an immediate choice that one entire source must be discarded.

The same applies to ordinary material. A small domestic assemblage may address eating, repair or disposal practices that a political chronicle does not discuss. Its historical value is not reduced because the objects are less visually impressive than a monument or because the society also produced writing.

Studies that establish context and chronology, including research on later phases in Swat, demonstrate why period labels alone are insufficient. “Medieval” covers questions, places and times that have to be specified. A shared label does not make all deposits contemporary.
An archive wider than antiquity

For heritage discovery, this perspective broadens what deserves attention. A later settlement, industrial feature or altered urban building can be archaeologically informative without pretending to be prehistoric. Age is not the only measure of evidential value.

It also changes how repair and clearance are understood. Later layers are not automatically obstructions covering a more important ancient story. They may contain the evidence needed to explain how a place continued, changed or was remembered.

Historical archaeology therefore works through a conversation between records rather than a competition between disciplines. The strongest account states what each source can establish, where they agree and where the difference itself becomes a question worth investigating.

title: Old excavation reports: valuable records with limits
summary: Early excavation reports preserve observations that may no longer be recoverable. Reading them critically means separating documentation from inherited terminology and historical assumptions.

body.text: An old excavation report can be indispensable without being the last word. It may preserve a plan, a find location or a photograph of material that has since changed. At the same time, its classifications and explanations belong to the research habits of its period.
Preserve the observation, examine the claim

Ernest Mackay's report on Chanhudaro describes excavation levels, buildings and objects, but also makes broad claims about peoples and cultural change. A present-day reader should not reproduce its racial or evolutionary language as neutral description. The task is to distinguish what the excavator recorded from the historical explanation attached to it.

That distinction need not diminish the report's value. A documented association can remain important even when an interpretation is revised. A drawing can preserve useful detail while its caption uses a name no longer accepted. Critical reading allows those different parts of the record to be assessed separately.

Begin with the publication's identity. Is it a preliminary account, a final excavation report, a catalogue or a later synthesis? A preliminary statement may reflect incomplete analysis. Quoting it without its status can make a provisional suggestion appear more settled than the author intended.
Classifications also have histories

Kenoyer's discussion of Indus beads explains how influential early typologies shaped later research and why additional technological observations can refine them. The point is not simply that newer work is better. It is that a familiar classification may contain assumptions that have become difficult to see through repeated use.

When comparing publications, check whether the same term means the same thing. A category defined by appearance in one study may be defined through manufacturing technique in another. Counting both together without examining those definitions can create an artificial pattern.

Modern reporting guidance from the Chartered Institute for Archaeologists stresses explicit attributes and explained codes. That principle helps readers approach older documentation too: abbreviations, catalogue numbers and figure references are part of the evidence trail, not disposable clutter.
Revisions should be traceable

If a later researcher changes a date or identification, the archive should show the basis for that revision. Was new material excavated? Was an existing object re-examined? Did the chronological framework change? These are different reasons and should not disappear into the phrase “now believed”.

A digital archive can support this by keeping the early report linked to later work. It should neither delete the earlier interpretation nor repeat it without qualification. Readers can then see how knowledge developed rather than encountering a collection of apparently incompatible facts.

Old reports deserve particular care because some observations cannot be repeated. Excavation changes the ground, collections can become dispersed and landscapes can be altered. Preserving the report's information while questioning its assumptions is therefore not disloyal to earlier scholarship. It is how the record remains useful for questions its first authors may never have imagined.

title: From sherd to published argument
summary: A pottery fragment becomes evidence through a chain of recording, classification and comparison. Each step should remain visible when a published argument moves from a sherd to a wider historical claim.

body.text: A sherd is a fragment, not a miniature complete pot. It may preserve a rim, a base, part of a handle or an otherwise unremarkable piece of wall. Its contribution to a historical argument depends on what survives and on the information recorded with it.
Begin with attributes

Pottery recording guidance from the Chartered Institute for Archaeologists distinguishes contextual unit, fabric, form, decoration and other attributes. “Fabric” concerns the material body of the pottery, including its clay and inclusions; it does not mean a textile. This vocabulary allows researchers to describe comparable features rather than rely on an overall impression.

A fragment with a recognisable rim can offer different information from a plain body sherd. Decoration may support comparison, but it is not the only relevant feature. Material and manufacturing observations can complicate an identification that initially seemed obvious from colour or pattern.

The analytical advantage is that a description can be checked. Another specialist may disagree with the classification while still working from the recorded attributes. If the entry contains only a culture name, the reasoning that led to it becomes much harder to assess.
A fragment is not a vessel count

Several sherds may come from one vessel, while a small assemblage can also contain fragments of many different vessels. Counting pieces is therefore not identical to counting pots. The chosen measure needs to be stated before quantities are used to compare deposits or settlements.

This matters when an argument moves from pottery to behaviour. A higher fragment count does not automatically mean more people, more consumption or a longer occupation. Breakage, disposal and the composition of the investigated deposit all need consideration.

Reporting guidance also asks researchers to address condition and fragmentation when discussing how an assemblage formed. The published table and the interpretation should therefore belong to the same argument, rather than the table serving merely as a technical appendix no one is expected to read.
From comparison to historical explanation

A resemblance between two pottery groups may support a chronological or technological comparison. It does not independently prove migration, trade or shared identity. Those explanations require additional evidence and an account of why alternative mechanisms are less convincing.

For an archive reader encountering a sherd from a Pakistani mound, useful questions are modest and precise. Which part of the vessel survives? How securely is its context known? Is the proposed comparison based on form, fabric, decoration or several features together? What uncertainty remains?
The fragment's value is not diminished if the answer stops short of a dramatic story. A carefully documented sherd can refine a sequence or reveal a problem in an existing classification.

The route from fragment to argument should remain inspectable at every stage. Description, grouping, comparison and interpretation are connected operations, but they should not collapse into one confident label that hides how much work the conclusion actually requires.

title: How a Mughal charbagh organises movement
summary: A charbagh is experienced through routes, thresholds and changing views as well as symmetry. Lahore's Shalamar Gardens show why water and levels belong to the same architectural reading.

body.text: From a plan, a Mughal garden can appear to be an exercise in symmetry. On foot, the experience is less static: an entrance frames a view, a channel establishes direction and a change of level alters the relationship between water and architecture. The garden is organised through movement as well as geometry.
Axes are routes and sightlines

A charbagh is associated with a divided garden layout, but the term should not replace attention to a particular site. UNESCO describes Shalamar's upper and lower terraces through square arrangements and its intermediate terrace through a narrower configuration. The three levels do not offer an identical experience.

An axis can guide the eye without functioning everywhere as an unrestricted path. A basin, platform or threshold may interrupt movement while extending a visual line. Reading the garden therefore involves asking where a visitor could walk, where a view continued and where access was mediated by architecture.

The distinction is especially useful when a photograph presents a long, apparently continuous perspective. The image may compress changes of level or conceal a crossing. A plan and a view should be read together rather than allowing either to supply the whole experience.
Water is part of the arrangement

Water features establish relationships among channels, basins, platforms and pavilions. Their historical significance is not limited to decoration or symbolism. Their position also helps structure the route through the garden and the places from which it is seen.

The Mughal Gardens research project presents Shalamar within a broader architectural landscape. ICOMOS's conservation discussion, meanwhile, treats the garden as a historic entity requiring care. Together they encourage a reading in which buildings, planting and waterworks are interdependent rather than separate attractions.

That interdependence is also a caution about reconstruction. A dry channel today is evidence of a surviving feature, not an adequate demonstration of every effect it once produced. Conversely, a functioning modern water display should not be assumed to reproduce an original hydraulic arrangement without documentation.
Thresholds make distinctions

A gateway or terrace boundary can change the scale and character of the space beyond it. Such transitions invite questions about ceremony, access and the relationship between different parts of a royal setting. Specific historical claims about who used each area still need documentary support.

For visitors, an attentive walk can begin with simple observations: where does a path turn, what becomes visible at a crossing, and which building anchors the view? These observations do not require assigning a symbolic meaning to every tree or pool.

The premium quality of the garden lies partly in these carefully composed relationships. A charbagh is not merely a diagram reproduced on the ground. At Shalamar, levels, routes and water create a sequence that has to be experienced through time. Understanding that sequence makes the garden's architectural intelligence visible beyond its most familiar postcard view.

title: The pavilion: a small building with several jobs
summary: A pavilion can mark a destination, frame a view or organise an approach. Hiran Minar's tank setting shows why a small building must be read through its wider composition.

body.text: A pavilion may occupy little ground while organising a much larger setting. Its significance can depend on how it is approached, what it overlooks and how its openings connect interior and exterior. Describing it simply as a small decorative building misses those relationships.
Hiran Minar's building in the water

Pakistan's Tentative List description of Hiran Minar and Tank identifies an octagonal pavilion in the tank, reached by a causeway. It also records square pavilions at the corners. The central and corner structures belong to one composition, but they occupy different positions within it.

That arrangement gives the approach architectural importance. The central pavilion is not reached in the same way as a roadside room. Its relationship with the water and the causeway makes movement towards it part of the experience. A photograph of the building alone can hide precisely what makes its setting distinctive.

The official description uses the term baradari for the central pavilion. It does not follow that every open-sided building in every heritage garden should receive the same name. A recorded local or historical designation is preferable to a label supplied solely because the structure looks picturesque.
Position can change the job

A comparison outside Pakistan helps clarify the point without merging the sites. The government description of Humayun's tomb places a pavilion along the eastern enclosure of the garden complex. A building positioned on a boundary relates to routes and views differently from one standing within a tank.

This does not establish that the two structures had identical uses or patrons' intentions. It shows why “pavilion” describes a broad architectural category rather than a complete functional history. To understand a particular example, the reader needs its plan, access and documented context.

Some functions may be visible in the arrangement; others require historical evidence. A platform can provide a place to pause, but an account of a specific ceremony cannot be inferred from that possibility. Shelter, display and viewing may overlap, yet their balance should not be invented for an unnamed occasion.
Read the openings, not just the roof

The number and position of openings determine which directions are visually connected. Steps, railings and changes of level can shape how a person occupies the space. These details are often more informative than assigning a style name after a quick glance at the roofline.

Conservation and later alteration may change those relationships. An opening that is blocked today or a route that has been redirected should not be silently projected into the building's earliest phase. A heritage account can identify the current condition while explaining what is historically documented.

Hiran Minar's pavilion is consequently best understood with its tank and approach, not extracted from them. Its scale may be modest compared with the landscape it commands, but that is exactly the architectural achievement: a small structure giving focus to a much larger experience.

title: A courtyard is more than empty space
summary: A courtyard connects rooms through light, routes and views. Reading domestic architecture requires attention to how the open centre works, not just to the ornament around it.

body.text: The centre of a courtyard house can seem to be the part where nothing has been built. In architectural terms, that apparent emptiness is active. Rooms face it, routes pass through or around it, and openings connect spaces that would otherwise be separated by walls.
The centre belongs to the plan

Sethi House in Peshawar is documented in official heritage material, including the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa archaeology report's courtyard view. The image offers a useful starting point for looking at the relationship between an open centre and its surrounding elevations. It does not, on its own, explain every room's historical use.

The first question is how the house is entered. Does the approach reveal the court immediately, or does a threshold interrupt the view? Then consider how rooms connect with the centre and with one another. A court can distribute movement without every room needing to open directly onto a street.

Vertical relationships matter as well. An upper-level opening may overlook the same court from a different position. That shared visual space does not mean that access to every level was identical. A photograph can show architectural connections while leaving the social arrangements unresolved.
Light, shade and daily activity

An open court admits daylight, but its effect depends on the height and orientation of the surrounding building. A narrow, tall enclosure and a broad, low one cannot be assumed to behave in the same way. The word “courtyard” identifies a spatial relationship, not a universal environmental formula.

Claims about cooling require similar care. Shade, airflow, materials and water can interact, but a general statement that all old houses were naturally comfortable conceals variation. The useful approach is to study the particular arrangement rather than turn the courtyard into an effortless answer to every climatic problem.

Daily uses may also change over time. A space might accommodate several activities at different hours, yet assigning those activities to a named historic family requires evidence. Architecture can suggest possibilities without giving us permission to script domestic scenes.
Ornament does not replace circulation

Carved wood, painted surfaces and decorative openings often dominate photographs of historic houses. They deserve attention, but their relationship with the plan matters. An elaborately treated opening may also frame a route or mediate a view. Seeing only its ornament removes part of its architectural work.

WCLA's presentation of Lahore's historic environment offers another route into domestic and urban settings, but individual houses should not be treated as interchangeable examples of one timeless way of life. Sethi House, Haveli Sujan Singh and Haveli Nau Nihal Singh each require their own documented history.

A good courtyard account therefore begins with relationships that can be observed and identifies the evidence behind broader social claims. The open centre becomes more than a photogenic void: it is the space through which much of the building's organisation can be understood, while the lives once arranged around it remain a subject for careful historical inquiry.

title: From square room to dome: squinches and pendentives
summary: Squinches and pendentives address the transition between a chamber and a dome. Learning the distinction helps readers describe what they see without turning one feature into an unsupported date.

body.text: Look up inside a domed chamber and the most revealing part may not be the dome's centre. It can be the zone where the room's corners meet the structure above. A square plan and a circular dome do not share the same outline, so their relationship has to be resolved architecturally.
Two terms for a transition

A squinch bridges or occupies a corner, helping transform the support above a square space into a form that can carry the dome. A pendentive is a curved triangular transition associated with the space between supporting arches. Architectural teaching material distinguishes these approaches because their geometry is not the same.

Patricia Blessing's Khamseen presentation treats squinch and pendentive together as terms in Islamic architectural history. The comparison is useful for looking, but it should not become a competition in which every building must be placed in one simple box after a single photograph.

Decoration can complicate recognition. A surface may be richly articulated, while the structural relationship beneath it is less obvious. An ornate corner should not automatically be identified as one device simply because it resembles an illustration seen elsewhere.
Follow the room upwards

Begin with the plan. Where are the main supports, and what happens at the corners? Does the transition appear as a distinct feature across a corner, or as part of a continuous curved surface between arches? Then ask how the zone above changes before the dome begins.

These questions can be explored through measured sections and clear photographs. A low-angle interior image may hide the junction, while an exterior view can reveal little about the internal transition. If the evidence is insufficient, an honest description can identify the problem without forcing a label.

The distinction also warns against dating a building from one feature. A constructional solution can be used in different regions and periods. Identifying it is one step in analysis, not a complete chronology or proof of a direct line of influence between two monuments.
Compare without importing an answer

For Pakistani mosques and tombs, the terms are useful when supported by documentation of the specific building. A related place in an atlas is an invitation to examine evidence, not a claim that its interior has already been structurally classified.

A reliable account should separate the visible surface from the interpretation of how it carries loads. This article offers vocabulary for understanding published drawings, not an engineering assessment or permission to enter restricted structural spaces.

Once the transition is noticed, the chamber becomes easier to read as a three-dimensional composition. The dome is no longer a shape placed mysteriously above four walls. It belongs to a sequence of supports, surfaces and spatial adjustments.

That sequence is the real value of the vocabulary. Naming a squinch or pendentive should sharpen attention to the building, not end the investigation with a term that sounds more certain than the available view.

title: The dome and the roof are not always the same shell
summary: An exterior dome need not reproduce the ceiling seen inside. Double-shell construction separates two architectural profiles, but a particular building needs documented evidence before receiving that label.

body.text: A dome seen across a skyline can appear taller or differently shaped than the ceiling experienced inside the chamber below it. That difference does not necessarily mean one view is misleading. In double-shell construction, the interior and exterior profiles can belong to distinct shells rather than opposite faces of one continuous thickness.
Two profiles, different experiences

The Government of Delhi's description of Humayun's tomb identifies its prominent double dome. It provides a documented comparative example for understanding the term. It does not establish that every visually similar dome in Pakistan has the same construction.

The architectural distinction is useful because the interior and exterior answer different spatial demands. A chamber is experienced from within, through its proportions and surfaces. A roof or dome also contributes to the building's distant silhouette. Separate shells can allow those profiles to differ rather than requiring one shape to serve both experiences identically.

That is an explanation of the principle, not a reconstruction of the engineering of every double dome. Materials, connections and construction histories need building-specific evidence. An elegant diagram is not a substitute for a documented section.
What a photograph cannot establish

A bulbous outline alone is not proof of double-shell construction. Nor does a difference between an interior photograph and an exterior photograph necessarily settle the matter: the views may be difficult to compare, and later alterations may complicate the relationship.

Measured drawings can clarify what a casual view cannot. Historic England's recording guidance distinguishes levels and methods of documentation for understanding buildings. The wider methodological lesson is relevant here: a description should state the evidence behind a structural identification.

A useful section needs to show which surfaces were measured and which were inferred. If a cavity was inaccessible, that limitation should be recorded. The most visually complete drawing is not automatically the most reliable unless its conventions and basis are clear.
Keep the local question open

Attock Tomb and Marhi Baba Dhyghana Singh may appear in a comparative heritage route concerned with domed architecture. Their inclusion should not be read as an unsupported assertion that both have a particular shell arrangement. Each requires its own technical documentation and chronology.

The distinction is also important in conservation. A crack or moisture stain on an interior surface does not, by itself, diagnose the condition of every part above it. Assessment belongs to qualified professionals with access to the relevant structure, not to an improvised interpretation from a visitor photograph.

For the interested reader, the reward is a more exact question: which surface am I looking at, and how does it relate to the building's other profile? That question turns a familiar silhouette into an investigation of architectural depth.
The dome is not always a single object with one shape. Learning to distinguish appearance from documented construction makes both the skyline and the room beneath it more intelligible.

title: Reading a shikhara without guessing a date
summary: A shikhara belongs to an architectural composition, not a ready-made date label. Salt Range temple research shows the value of regional comparison and careful attention to surviving fabric.

body.text: The rising superstructure of a temple can dominate its appearance so completely that the rest of the building becomes a supporting detail. The term shikhara helps describe an important part of temple architecture, but it should not become a shortcut that assigns a date or dynasty from a silhouette alone.
A regional sequence, not an isolated shape

Michael W. Meister's study of temples along the Indus presents the Salt Range material through an integrated architectural and archaeological investigation. He identifies a distinctive regional tradition and examines its relationship with wider architectural forms. The argument depends on a corpus of buildings, not one tower recognised from a distance.

His discussion of Malot is especially useful for understanding comparison. The temple's relationship with architectural traditions in Kashmir is considered through specific formal features and historical context. That is more precise than treating every temple in the region as an interchangeable instance of a broad style.

Later scholarship on the Salt Range also discusses how earlier surveys and classifications shaped the field. Architectural terms have research histories. A label can be useful while still needing explanation about which features it groups together and which differences it leaves visible.
Read from the base to the top

A temple's plan, wall articulation, projections, mouldings and surviving superstructure contribute to its interpretation. Looking only at the highest element can conceal the evidence offered by lower parts of the building. A damaged top may also distort the impression of the original profile.

A careful description should identify what survives. Does the account concern intact masonry, fragments, an early photograph or a scholarly reconstruction? These sources can be combined, but their different status should not disappear when a drawing is reproduced.

Chronology requires a further step. A formal resemblance may support a comparison, yet resemblance alone does not establish the exact date of construction. Inscriptions, archaeological context and a reasoned regional sequence can strengthen or revise an attribution.
Avoid the timeless temple image

Sites such as Katas Raj, Malot and Harnoli should not be collapsed into one undated visual tradition simply because they are all described as temples. Their individual histories, conditions and available documentation differ. A heritage category is a starting point for discovery, not a conclusion about chronology.

The same care applies to religious continuity. A surviving form does not automatically establish that use was uninterrupted, nor does damage prove that all associations with the place ended. Architectural and community histories need their own evidence.

For a visitor, a useful exercise is to move attention away from the summit. Notice how the entrance, walls and base organise the building before returning to the tower. Then compare those observations with a published plan or study.

The shikhara becomes more informative when it is restored to the composition around it. Vocabulary should help readers see relationships and ask better questions, not supply an instant date that the building itself has not been shown to support.
